newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Defectors say North Korea boosts border security.
newsitem.headline: Defectors say North Korea boosts border security.

text.p: The biggest group of defectors to flee North Korea gave a first news conference on Tuesday saying the impoverished nation had nearly tripled guards along its borders with China and Russia to stop escapees.
They also said North Koreans had been advised to prepare for possible chemical, biological and nuclear warfare by making and keeping at home clothes and devices to protect themselves.

"The number of personnel at each border post has been raised to 20 from eight," said Choi Young-ho, a North Korean border guard who guided the other 16 defectors, all from one family, across the Tumen River on the border with China.

Choi, 30, who described himself as a friend of Kim Kum-chol, eldest son of the family of 16, said the number of border posts had also been increased to one every two kilometres from one every four kilometres since September.
Earlier media reports said Choi was a cousin of the family.
The band of men, women and young children arrived in Seoul on December 9 to seek asylum after a six weeks-long epic escape down the length of China and into Hong Kong.
They crossed into China on October 26 and reached Hong Kong on November 23.
In a report that could not be verified, Lee Hye-young, wife of Kim Kum-chol, said hunger was so widespread that some women ate their own placenta after giving birth to get protein.
Lee also said that last September people were told to get ready for chemical, biological and nuclear warfare by having a "kit ready just in case."
She said households were advised to have plastic eyeglasses, gloves, caps, and face masks.
Choi Hyon-sil, 57, reversed earlier remarks by her father in New York that the family carried poison to commit suicide if they were caught.
"I had told my family 'Let's prepare some rat poision', but in the end we did not actually carry poison," Choi said.

She said she carried 20 sleeping tablets and planned to give them to the children to keep them quiet when the band crossed the Tumen River. But the precaution was not needed and the tablets were not used.

The group said people who had lived through the 1950-53 Korean War as well as government and party officials had a "negative" view of a new conflict with rival South Korea because they knew what could be the tragic results.
But Kim Myong-suk, 34, said many ordinary people were in such despair about the country's food shortages and poverty they did not care about their fate.
"It's the same to die in a war or in a famine," he said.

During the conference, Kim Kum-hyok, aged three, the youngest of the defectors, gave an immediate recitation of a poem which his mother explained the nation had to learn to mark the 50th birthday of North Korean leader Kim Jong-il.
The defectors said as part of an "idolisation" campaign of Kim, the population every Tuesday sings some of 100 songs praising him.
The group gave few details of their journey through China because they said they did not want to get into trouble any of the two million ethnic Koreans living there.
The band moved from one safe house to another in their trip which took them through the Chinese cities of Yanbian, Shenyang and Beijing.
Officials from Seoul's Agency for National Security Planning also requested journalists to abstain from asking for details about the journey, citing diplomatic relations with China.
